explanation:
## What the grids show

Each input is a black (0) 9×9 field with a few isolated grey (5) cells. In the outputs the grey cells are still in place. Every one of them now sits at the centre of a 3×3 square whose other eight cells are blue (1). Nothing else changes.

The fact sheet supports this:

- **Pair 1:** 4 grey cells give 4 blue objects of size 8 each, so 32 cells change. That is exactly 4 rings of 8.
- **Pair 2:** two of the rings touch diagonally, at (5,2)/(6,2), and merge into one blue object of size 16. The other ring is separate (size 8). So 3 rings give 24 changed cells.
- **Clipping:** rings that would hang off the grid are cut at the border. In pair 1 the grey at (1,7) has a ring reaching row 0 and column 8, which are edge cells, so nothing is cut. In pair 2 the grey at (7,1) has a ring reaching column 0, also still inside. The code clips anyway, so a grey on the border would still work.
- **Only black is painted:** the only colour change anywhere is 0→1. The rule paints only background cells and never overwrites a grey.

## Rule

For every grey (non-background) cell, paint the 8 surrounding cells blue (1), clipped to the grid. Only background cells are painted.

## Applying it to the test

The test has five grey cells: (1,1), (2,7), (4,3), (7,1) and (7,5).

- Each one gets its own 3×3 blue ring.
- The rings around (1,1) and (4,3) meet at the corner cell (2,2)/(3,2). This is harmless: overlaps just paint blue on blue.
- No ring reaches past the grid edge.

I emit one stage per stamped ring, plus the final canvas.
